claim: N6-methyladenosine (m6A) is the most abundant internal modification of eukaryotic messenger RNA (mRNA).
source: N6-methyladenosine (m6A) is the most abundant internal modification of eukaryotic messenger RNA (mRNA) and plays critical roles in RNA biology.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field of RNA biology, representing established scientific consensus.

claim: m6A plays critical roles in RNA biology.
source: N6-methyladenosine (m6A) is the most abundant internal modification of eukaryotic messenger RNA (mRNA) and plays critical roles in RNA biology.
evidence: This is supported by established scientific knowledge and the broader context of the manuscript.

claim: The function of m6A modification is mediated by m6A-selective 'reader' proteins of the YTH family.
source: The function of this modification is mediated by m6A-selective 'reader' proteins of the YTH family, which incorporate m6A-modified mRNAs into pathways of RNA metabolism.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work and established knowledge in the field.

claim: YTH family reader proteins incorporate m6A-modified mRNAs into pathways of RNA metabolism.
source: The function of this modification is mediated by m6A-selective 'reader' proteins of the YTH family, which incorporate m6A-modified mRNAs into pathways of RNA metabolism.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge and citations in the introduction.

claim: YTHDC1 mediates export of methylated mRNA from the nucleus to the cytoplasm in HeLa cells.
source: Here, we show that the m6A-binding protein YTHDC1 mediates export of methylated mRNA from the nucleus to the cytoplasm in HeLa cells.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the study, supported by multiple experimental data presented in the manuscript including LC-MS/MS, RNA-seq, and nascent RNA labeling experiments.

claim: Knockdown of YTHDC1 results in an extended residence time for nuclear m6A-containing mRNA.
source: Knockdown of YTHDC1 results in an extended residence time for nuclear m6A-containing mRNA, with an accumulation of transcripts in the nucleus and accompanying depletion within the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and related experiments.

claim: Knockdown of YTHDC1 results in accumulation of transcripts in the nucleus.
source: Knockdown of YTHDC1 results in an extended residence time for nuclear m6A-containing mRNA, with an accumulation of transcripts in the nucleus and accompanying depletion within the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data including LC-MS/MS (Figure 2A), polyA imaging (Figure 2C, D), and RNA-seq (Figure 3B).

claim: Knockdown of YTHDC1 results in depletion of m6A-containing transcripts within the cytoplasm.
source: Knockdown of YTHDC1 results in an extended residence time for nuclear m6A-containing mRNA, with an accumulation of transcripts in the nucleus and accompanying depletion within the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data including LC-MS/MS (Figure 2A) and RNA-seq (Figure 3C).

claim: YTHDC1 interacts with the splicing factor and nuclear export adaptor protein SRSF3.
source: YTHDC1 interacts with the splicing factor and nuclear export adaptor protein SRSF3, and facilitates RNA binding to both SRSF3 and NXF1.
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: YTHDC1 facilitates RNA binding to SRSF3.
source: YTHDC1 interacts with the splicing factor and nuclear export adaptor protein SRSF3, and facilitates RNA binding to both SRSF3 and NXF1.
evidence: This is supported by CLIP-seq experiments showing reduced SRSF3 binding to target RNAs upon YTHDC1 knockdown (Figure 6A, B).

claim: YTHDC1 facilitates RNA binding to NXF1.
source: YTHDC1 interacts with the splicing factor and nuclear export adaptor protein SRSF3, and facilitates RNA binding to both SRSF3 and NXF1.
evidence: This is supported by RIP-seq experiments showing reduced NXF1 binding to target RNAs upon YTHDC1 knockdown (Figure 6C, D).

claim: YTHDC1's role in mRNA export expands the potential utility of chemical modification of mRNA.
source: This role for YTHDC1 expands the potential utility of chemical modification of mRNA, and supports an emerging paradigm of m6A as a distinct biochemical entity for selective processing and metabolism of mammalian mRNAs.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: m6A functions as a distinct biochemical entity for selective processing and metabolism of mammalian mRNAs.
source: This role for YTHDC1 expands the potential utility of chemical modification of mRNA, and supports an emerging paradigm of m6A as a distinct biochemical entity for selective processing and metabolism of mammalian mRNAs.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data showing selective effects on m6A-containing transcripts and represents an interpretation of the findings.

claim: YTHDF1 and YTHDF2 facilitate m6A-dependent translation initiation and m6A-dependent mRNA decay, respectively, under normal and stress conditions.
source: Within the cytoplasm, YTHDF1 and YTHDF2 facilitate m6A-dependent translation initiation and m6A-dependent mRNA decay, respectively, under normal and stress conditions (Batista et al., 2014; Du et al., 2016; Geula et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2014a, 2014b, 2015; Zhou et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior published work.

claim: eIF3 has roles in m6A-based regulation of cap-independent translation.
source: Additional roles in m6A-based regulation of cap-independent translation have been described for eIF3 as well as for the catalytic methyltransferase component METTL3, each functioning to promote the translation of methylated mRNAs (Lin et al., 2016; Meyer et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: METTL3 has roles in m6A-based regulation of cap-independent translation.
source: Additional roles in m6A-based regulation of cap-independent translation have been described for eIF3 as well as for the catalytic methyltransferase component METTL3, each functioning to promote the translation of methylated mRNAs (Lin et al., 2016; Meyer et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: YTHDC1, HNRNPA2B1 and HNRNPC bind to m6A-modified RNAs and facilitate splice site selection.
source: Within the nucleus, YTHDC1, HNRNPA2B1 and HNRNPC bind to m6A-modified RNAs and facilitate splice site selection (Alarcón et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2015; Xiao et al., 2016; Xu et al., 2014), individual examples of which are required for vertebrate development (Haussmann et al., 2016; Lence et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior published work.

claim: Individual examples of m6A-dependent splice site selection are required for vertebrate development.
source: Within the nucleus, YTHDC1, HNRNPA2B1 and HNRNPC bind to m6A-modified RNAs and facilitate splice site selection (Alarcón et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2015; Xiao et al., 2016; Xu et al., 2014), individual examples of which are required for vertebrate development (Haussmann et al., 2016; Lence et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: The relationship between m6A methylation and other nuclear events has yet to be investigated fully.
source: However, the relationship between m6A methylation and other nuclear events has yet to be investigated fully.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field at the time of writing.

claim: The direct link between nuclear mRNA processing and the pool of cytoplasmic transcripts available for translation in the cytoplasm has remained elusive.
source: Specifically, the direct link between nuclear mRNA processing and the pool of cytoplasmic transcripts available for translation in the cytoplasm has remained elusive.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field at the time of writing, providing context for the study.

claim: The physical segregation of biological processes into nuclear and cytoplasmic compartments is a fundamental feature of eukaryotic organisms.
source: The physical segregation of biological processes into nuclear and cytoplasmic compartments is a fundamental feature of eukaryotic organisms, and necessitates efficient systems for shuttling mRNA to sites of active translation.
evidence: This is established biological knowledge.

claim: Physical segregation of nuclear and cytoplasmic compartments necessitates efficient systems for shuttling mRNA to sites of active translation.
source: The physical segregation of biological processes into nuclear and cytoplasmic compartments is a fundamental feature of eukaryotic organisms, and necessitates efficient systems for shuttling mRNA to sites of active translation.
evidence: This is a logical inference from established biological knowledge.

claim: The functional coupling of transcription, 5' capping, splicing, 3' polyadenylation, and nuclear export of mRNA ensures that genetic information is properly passed from DNA to protein.
source: The functional coupling of the transcription, 5' capping, splicing, 3' polyadenylation, and nuclear export of mRNA ensures that genetic information is properly passed from DNA to protein (Moore and Proudfoot, 2009), as exemplified by the scaffolding functions of RNA polymerase II throughout transcription (Egloff and Murphy, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: RNA polymerase II has scaffolding functions throughout transcription.
source: The functional coupling of the transcription, 5' capping, splicing, 3' polyadenylation, and nuclear export of mRNA ensures that genetic information is properly passed from DNA to protein (Moore and Proudfoot, 2009), as exemplified by the scaffolding functions of RNA polymerase II throughout transcription (Egloff and Murphy, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: The existence of multifunctional adaptor proteins that have roles in pre-mRNA splicing and export of mature mRNA suggests that mRNA nuclear processing and transport are regulated by the dynamics of protein–RNA interactions in eukaryotes.
source: The existence of multifunctional adaptor proteins that have roles in the pre-mRNA splicing and export of mature mRNA suggests that mRNA nuclear processing and transport are regulated by the dynamics of protein–RNA interactions in eukaryotes (Huang and Steitz, 2001; Huang et al., 2003; Müller-McNicoll et al., 2016; Rodrigues et al., 2001; Strässer and Hurt, 2001; Valencia et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior published work.

claim: The regulation of mRNA export occurs in response to various stimuli.
source: It has become clear that the regulation of mRNA export occurs in response to various stimuli, and is affected by both cis elements within mRNA sequences and the specificity of trans factors such as RNA-binding proteins (Carmody et al., 2009; Wickramasinghe and Laskey, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: mRNA export is affected by cis elements within mRNA sequences.
source: It has become clear that the regulation of mRNA export occurs in response to various stimuli, and is affected by both cis elements within mRNA sequences and the specificity of trans factors such as RNA-binding proteins (Carmody et al., 2009; Wickramasinghe and Laskey, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: mRNA export is affected by the specificity of trans factors such as RNA-binding proteins.
source: It has become clear that the regulation of mRNA export occurs in response to various stimuli, and is affected by both cis elements within mRNA sequences and the specificity of trans factors such as RNA-binding proteins (Carmody et al., 2009; Wickramasinghe and Laskey, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: m6A modification of mRNA has emerged as a previously unrecognized regulator of RNA structure.
source: Within the nucleus, m6A modification of mRNA has emerged as a previously unrecognized regulator of RNA structure (Liu et al., 2015; Spitale et al., 2015) and of protein–RNA interactions.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: m6A modification of mRNA has emerged as a previously unrecognized regulator of protein–RNA interactions.
source: Within the nucleus, m6A modification of mRNA has emerged as a previously unrecognized regulator of RNA structure (Liu et al., 2015; Spitale et al., 2015) and of protein–RNA interactions.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior published work and the broader context of the manuscript.

claim: m6A has long been considered to play critical roles in constitutive splicing.
source: m6A has long been considered to play critical roles in constitutive splicing as well as in processing-linked transport of cellular and viral mRNAs (Finkel and Groner, 1983; Fustin et al., 2013; Lichinchi et al., 2016; Stoltzfus and Dane, 1982), suggesting fundamental roles for mRNA methylation within the nucleus in addition to those in pre-mRNA splicing.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: m6A has long been considered to play critical roles in processing-linked transport of cellular and viral mRNAs.
source: m6A has long been considered to play critical roles in constitutive splicing as well as in processing-linked transport of cellular and viral mRNAs (Finkel and Groner, 1983; Fustin et al., 2013; Lichinchi et al., 2016; Stoltzfus and Dane, 1982), suggesting fundamental roles for mRNA methylation within the nucleus in addition to those in pre-mRNA splicing.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Treatment with S-tubercidinylhomocysteine (STH) reduces m6A levels by over 80% in HeLa cells.
source: Treatment with the S-adenosylhomocysteine analog S-tubercidinylhomocysteine (STH) reduces m6A levels by over 80% in HeLa cells and results in delayed nuclear export of mature mRNA (Camper et al., 1984), whereas depletion of the m6A demethylase ALKBH5 results in rapid cytoplasmic appearance of mRNA (Zheng et al., 2013), further suggesting that m6A is directly involved in nuclear-to-cytoplasmic localization.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: Treatment with S-tubercidinylhomocysteine (STH) results in delayed nuclear export of mature mRNA.
source: Treatment with the S-adenosylhomocysteine analog S-tubercidinylhomocysteine (STH) reduces m6A levels by over 80% in HeLa cells and results in delayed nuclear export of mature mRNA (Camper et al., 1984), whereas depletion of the m6A demethylase ALKBH5 results in rapid cytoplasmic appearance of mRNA (Zheng et al., 2013), further suggesting that m6A is directly involved in nuclear-to-cytoplasmic localization.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: Depletion of the m6A demethylase ALKBH5 results in rapid cytoplasmic appearance of mRNA.
source: Treatment with the S-adenosylhomocysteine analog S-tubercidinylhomocysteine (STH) reduces m6A levels by over 80% in HeLa cells and results in delayed nuclear export of mature mRNA (Camper et al., 1984), whereas depletion of the m6A demethylase ALKBH5 results in rapid cytoplasmic appearance of mRNA (Zheng et al., 2013), further suggesting that m6A is directly involved in nuclear-to-cytoplasmic localization.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: m6A is directly involved in nuclear-to-cytoplasmic localization.
source: Treatment with the S-adenosylhomocysteine analog S-tubercidinylhomocysteine (STH) reduces m6A levels by over 80% in HeLa cells and results in delayed nuclear export of mature mRNA (Camper et al., 1984), whereas depletion of the m6A demethylase ALKBH5 results in rapid cytoplasmic appearance of mRNA (Zheng et al., 2013), further suggesting that m6A is directly involved in nuclear-to-cytoplasmic localization.
evidence: This is an inference based on cited prior work.

claim: The underlying mechanism and pathway for m6A-dependent nuclear transport have never been revealed.
source: Despite evidence for m6A-dependent nuclear transport, the underlying mechanism and pathway have never been revealed.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field at the time of writing, providing context for the study.

claim: Binding by YTHDC1 promotes the redistribution of transcripts to the cytoplasm.
source: Knockdown of YTHDC1 results in nuclear accumulation of methylated mRNAs, accompanied by cytoplasmic depletion of these mRNAs in HeLa cells, whereas binding by YTHDC1 promotes the redistribution of transcripts to the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the reporter assay (Figure 4C, D, E, F).

claim: YTHDC1 incorporates target mRNAs into the nuclear export pathway by interaction with SRSF3.
source: YTHDC1 incorporates target mRNAs into the nuclear export pathway by interaction with SRSF3, delivering RNA to the splicing and adaptor protein.
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation data (Figure 5A, B) and functional data showing SRSF3 dependence (Figure 7A).

claim: Association of YTHDC1 targets with SRSF3 is required for YTHDC1-dependent export.
source: Association of YTHDC1 targets with SRSF3 is required for YTHDC1-dependent export.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data showing that only transcripts bound by both YTHDC1 and SRSF3 show significant nuclear accumulation upon YTHDC1 knockdown (Figure 7A).

claim: YTHDC1 utilizes known interactions with SRSF3 to selectively mediate the entry of methylated mRNAs into known routes for export to the cytoplasm.
source: By performing analysis of subcellular mRNA populations, we show that YTHDC1 utilizes known interactions with SRSF3 to selectively mediate the entry of methylated mRNAs into known routes for export to the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is supported by multiple lines of experimental data including subcellular RNA-seq, CLIP-seq, and protein interaction studies.

claim: m6A promotes the clearance of cytoplasmic and nuclear mRNAs.
source: m6A promotes the clearance of cytoplasmic and nuclear mRNAs and is known to facilitate rapid clearance of mRNAs from the cytoplasm due to direct binding of YTHDF2 and recruitment of the CCR4–NOT deadenylase complex (Du et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work and experimental data in Figure 1.

claim: m6A facilitates rapid clearance of mRNAs from the cytoplasm due to direct binding of YTHDF2 and recruitment of the CCR4–NOT deadenylase complex.
source: m6A promotes the clearance of cytoplasmic and nuclear mRNAs and is known to facilitate rapid clearance of mRNAs from the cytoplasm due to direct binding of YTHDF2 and recruitment of the CCR4–NOT deadenylase complex (Du et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Cells treated with control siRNA preferentially cleared m6A-containing mRNAs in the absence of new transcription.
source: Cells treated with control short interfering RNA (siRNA) preferentially cleared m6A-containing mRNAs, as indicated by a reduction in the m6A/A ratio in the absence of new transcription (Figure 1A, black).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Knockdown of YTHDF2 resulted in increased m6A levels at t=0 in cytoplasmic mRNA.
source: Knockdown of the cytoplasmic protein YTHDF2 resulted in increased m6A levels (t = 0), and extended the apparent half-life for m6A in cytoplasmic mRNA by ~4 fold (Figure 1A, gray, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), as would be expected in the absence of the m6A-specific mRNA decay factor.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Knockdown of YTHDF2 extended the apparent half-life for m6A in cytoplasmic mRNA by ~4 fold.
source: Knockdown of the cytoplasmic protein YTHDF2 resulted in increased m6A levels (t = 0), and extended the apparent half-life for m6A in cytoplasmic mRNA by ~4 fold (Figure 1A, gray, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), as would be expected in the absence of the m6A-specific mRNA decay factor.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Nuclear m6A levels in mRNA decreased over a six-hour time course following inhibition of transcription.
source: Following inhibition of transcription, nuclear m6A levels in mRNA decreased over a six-hour time course, suggesting that selective processing and clearance of these mRNAs is common to both the nuclear and the cytoplasmic compartments (Figure 1B, black).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Selective processing and clearance of m6A-containing mRNAs is common to both the nuclear and the cytoplasmic compartments.
source: Following inhibition of transcription, nuclear m6A levels in mRNA decreased over a six-hour time course, suggesting that selective processing and clearance of these mRNAs is common to both the nuclear and the cytoplasmic compartments (Figure 1B, black).
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data shown in Figure 1A and 1B.

claim: Knockdown of YTHDC1 resulted in increased m6A levels in nuclear mRNA at t=0.
source: Knockdown of the only nuclear member of the YTH family and known m6A-binding protein, YTHDC1, resulted in increased m6A levels in nuclear mRNA (t = 0) and in a decreased rate of clearance of m6A methylation in mRNA, extending the apparent half-life of methylation more than 2-fold (Figure 1B, red, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Knockdown of YTHDC1 resulted in a decreased rate of clearance of m6A methylation in nuclear mRNA.
source: Knockdown of the only nuclear member of the YTH family and known m6A-binding protein, YTHDC1, resulted in increased m6A levels in nuclear mRNA (t = 0) and in a decreased rate of clearance of m6A methylation in mRNA, extending the apparent half-life of methylation more than 2-fold (Figure 1B, red, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Knockdown of YTHDC1 extended the apparent half-life of m6A methylation in nuclear mRNA more than 2-fold.
source: Knockdown of the only nuclear member of the YTH family and known m6A-binding protein, YTHDC1, resulted in increased m6A levels in nuclear mRNA (t = 0) and in a decreased rate of clearance of m6A methylation in mRNA, extending the apparent half-life of methylation more than 2-fold (Figure 1B, red, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Analysis of mRNA from the nucleus showed no difference between control and YTHDF2 knockdown samples.
source: Analysis of mRNA from the nucleus showed no difference between control and YTHDF2 knockdown samples, confirming that the dominant role of YTHDF2 takes place in the cytoplasm under normal growth conditions (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The dominant role of YTHDF2 takes place in the cytoplasm under normal growth conditions.
source: Analysis of mRNA from the nucleus showed no difference between control and YTHDF2 knockdown samples, confirming that the dominant role of YTHDF2 takes place in the cytoplasm under normal growth conditions (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Knockdown of YTHDC1 resulted in decreased cytoplasmic levels of m6A at t=0.
source: Knockdown of YTHDC1 resulted in decreased cytoplasmic levels of m6A, but these levels approached control levels over the time course (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Cytoplasmic m6A levels approached control levels over the time course following YTHDC1 knockdown.
source: Knockdown of YTHDC1 resulted in decreased cytoplasmic levels of m6A, but these levels approached control levels over the time course (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: YTHDF2 mediates cytoplasmic decay of methylated mRNA transcripts.
source: These data suggest that while YTHDF2 mediates cytoplasmic decay of methylated mRNA transcripts, YTHDC1 mediates nuclear clearance of mRNAs and affects their resulting cytoplasmic abundance.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data shown in Figure 1 and supported by prior knowledge.

claim: YTHDC1 mediates nuclear clearance of mRNAs.
source: These data suggest that while YTHDF2 mediates cytoplasmic decay of methylated mRNA transcripts, YTHDC1 mediates nuclear clearance of mRNAs and affects their resulting cytoplasmic abundance.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: YTHDC1 affects the cytoplasmic abundance of mRNAs.
source: These data suggest that while YTHDF2 mediates cytoplasmic decay of methylated mRNA transcripts, YTHDC1 mediates nuclear clearance of mRNAs and affects their resulting cytoplasmic abundance.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Knockdown of YTHDC1 does not affect the m6A/A ratio in mRNA transcripts from whole cell lysate.
source: Knockdown of YTHDC1 does not affect the m6A/A ratio in mRNA transcripts from whole cell lysate, but results in accumulation of m6A in nuclear mRNA and in an accompanying cytoplasmic depletion of m6A levels (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Knockdown of YTHDC1 results in accumulation of m6A in nuclear mRNA.
source: Knockdown of YTHDC1 does not affect the m6A/A ratio in mRNA transcripts from whole cell lysate, but results in accumulation of m6A in nuclear mRNA and in an accompanying cytoplasmic depletion of m6A levels (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Knockdown of YTHDC1 results in cytoplasmic depletion of m6A levels.
source: Knockdown of YTHDC1 does not affect the m6A/A ratio in mRNA transcripts from whole cell lysate, but results in accumulation of m6A in nuclear mRNA and in an accompanying cytoplasmic depletion of m6A levels (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Knockdown of YTHDC1 does not affect the expression of YTHDF2.
source: These effects occurred without changes in the expression of YTHDF2, or of key components of the nuclear export machinery, the mRNA export receptor NXF1 or the adaptor protein ALYREF (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Knockdown of YTHDC1 does not affect the expression of NXF1.
source: These effects occurred without changes in the expression of YTHDF2, or of key components of the nuclear export machinery, the mRNA export receptor NXF1 or the adaptor protein ALYREF (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Knockdown of YTHDC1 does not affect the expression of ALYREF.
source: These effects occurred without changes in the expression of YTHDF2, or of key components of the nuclear export machinery, the mRNA export receptor NXF1 or the adaptor protein ALYREF (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: YTHDC1 knockdown results in increased polyA signal intensity in the nuclear region.
source: We can directly observe the effect of YTHDC1 knockdown on mRNA distribution by fluorescence in situ hybridization of polyA RNAs in HeLa cells, in which YTHDC1 knockdown results in increased signal intensity in the nuclear region and depletion in the cytoplasmic regions (Figure 2C and D), suggesting a positive role for YTHDC1 in nuclear mRNA export.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: YTHDC1 knockdown results in depletion of polyA signal in the cytoplasmic regions.
source: We can directly observe the effect of YTHDC1 knockdown on mRNA distribution by fluorescence in situ hybridization of polyA RNAs in HeLa cells, in which YTHDC1 knockdown results in increased signal intensity in the nuclear region and depletion in the cytoplasmic regions (Figure 2C and D), suggesting a positive role for YTHDC1 in nuclear mRNA export.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: YTHDC1 has a positive role in nuclear mRNA export.
source: We can directly observe the effect of YTHDC1 knockdown on mRNA distribution by fluorescence in situ hybridization of polyA RNAs in HeLa cells, in which YTHDC1 knockdown results in increased signal intensity in the nuclear region and depletion in the cytoplasmic regions (Figure 2C and D), suggesting a positive role for YTHDC1 in nuclear mRNA export.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: Overexpression of YTHDC1 reduced levels of m6A in nuclear mRNA.
source: Overexpression of YTHDC1 reduced levels of m6A in nuclear mRNA, suggesting that it contributes directly to the clearance of these transcripts, but did not result in increased levels of cytoplasmic m6A as anticipated (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: YTHDC1 contributes directly to the clearance of nuclear m6A-containing transcripts.
source: Overexpression of YTHDC1 reduced levels of m6A in nuclear mRNA, suggesting that it contributes directly to the clearance of these transcripts, but did not result in increased levels of cytoplasmic m6A as anticipated (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Overexpression of YTHDC1 did not result in increased levels of cytoplasmic m6A.
source: Overexpression of YTHDC1 reduced levels of m6A in nuclear mRNA, suggesting that it contributes directly to the clearance of these transcripts, but did not result in increased levels of cytoplasmic m6A as anticipated (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: YTHDC1 interacts with ZCCHC8.
source: Indeed, YTHDC1 has been reported to interact with ZCCHC8, a component of the NEXT complex (Lubas et al., 2011), an interaction that we verified by western Blot.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and a citation to prior work.

claim: YTHDC1 shows a robust interaction with ZCCHC8.
source: We found a robust interaction between YTHDC1 and ZCCHC8, but no interaction between YTHDC1 and MTR4 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: YTHDC1 shows no interaction with MTR4.
source: We found a robust interaction between YTHDC1 and ZCCHC8, but no interaction between YTHDC1 and MTR4 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Knockdown of ZCCHC8 and MTR4 did not produce an increase in nuclear RNA that is depleted for ribosomal transcripts.
source: Knockdown of these components did not produce an increase in nuclear RNA that is depleted for ribosomal transcripts (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: The accumulation of mature mRNA transcripts with YTHDC1 knockdown may not be attributed to nuclear decay.
source: These results suggest that the accumulation of mature mRNA transcripts with YTHDC1 knockdown may not be attributed to nuclear decay.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data showing no effect of NEXT/PAXT component knockdown.

claim: Overexpression of YTHDC1 following knockdown of YTHDF2 resulted in nuclear depletion of m6A.
source: We then overexpressed YTHDC1 following knockdown of YTHDF2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E). Under these conditions, we observed nuclear depletion as expected, as well as an increase in cytoplasmic m6A levels compared to empty vector control, suggesting that YTHDC1 mediates nuclear export of methylated mRNAs (Figure 2F) and that this nuclear localized protein can affect subcellular distribution of methylated transcripts (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Overexpression of YTHDC1 following knockdown of YTHDF2 resulted in an increase in cytoplasmic m6A levels compared to empty vector control.
source: We then overexpressed YTHDC1 following knockdown of YTHDF2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E). Under these conditions, we observed nuclear depletion as expected, as well as an increase in cytoplasmic m6A levels compared to empty vector control, suggesting that YTHDC1 mediates nuclear export of methylated mRNAs (Figure 2F) and that this nuclear localized protein can affect subcellular distribution of methylated transcripts (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: YTHDC1 can affect subcellular distribution of methylated transcripts.
source: We then overexpressed YTHDC1 following knockdown of YTHDF2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E). Under these conditions, we observed nuclear depletion as expected, as well as an increase in cytoplasmic m6A levels compared to empty vector control, suggesting that YTHDC1 mediates nuclear export of methylated mRNAs (Figure 2F) and that this nuclear localized protein can affect subcellular distribution of methylated transcripts (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Perturbations of YTHDC1 did not dramatically affect the incorporation of 4-thio-uridine in a 1-hr pulse period.
source: We compared the bulk transcriptional activity of HeLa cells treated with siRNA against YTHDC1 with control and YTHDC1-overexpressing lines, and found that these perturbations of YTHDC1 did not dramatically affect the incorporation of 4-thio-urudine in a 1-hr pulse period (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G and H), suggesting that YTHDC1 functions post-transcriptionally.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1G and H.

claim: YTHDC1 functions post-transcriptionally.
source: We compared the bulk transcriptional activity of HeLa cells treated with siRNA against YTHDC1 with control and YTHDC1-overexpressing lines, and found that these perturbations of YTHDC1 did not dramatically affect the incorporation of 4-thio-urudine in a 1-hr pulse period (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G and H), suggesting that YTHDC1 functions post-transcriptionally.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1G and H.

claim: Over 700 targets of YTHDC1 were identified using combined PAR-CLIP and RIP-seq data.
source: We identified targets as transcripts that were bound in each previous replicate of PAR-CLIP and enriched at least two-fold in each replicate of RIP-seq. These criteria produced over 700 targets of YTHDC1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Knockdown of YTHDC1 does not affect the abundance of target transcripts relative to non-target mRNAs in whole-cell samples.
source: Consistent with our mass spectrometry data, knockdown of YTHDC1 does not affect the abundance of target transcripts relative to non-target mRNAs in whole-cell samples (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Target abundance is unchanged from control levels in YTHDC1 knockdown cells in whole-cell samples.
source: Notably, target abundance is unchanged from control levels in YTHDC1 knockdown cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Target abundance is increased in nuclear RNA samples following knockdown of YTHDC1.
source: In the nuclear RNA sample, however, target abundance is increased following knockdown of YTHDC1, as indicated by a right shift in the cumulative fraction of these transcripts compared to non-target mRNAs (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: There is a decrease in cytoplasmic target abundance following knockdown of YTHDC1.
source: An accompanying decrease in cytoplasmic target abundance suggests that YTHDC1 mediates the subcellular distribution of its target mRNAs by promoting nuclear to cytoplasmic transport of bound transcripts (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: YTHDC1 mediates the subcellular distribution of its target mRNAs by promoting nuclear to cytoplasmic transport of bound transcripts.
source: An accompanying decrease in cytoplasmic target abundance suggests that YTHDC1 mediates the subcellular distribution of its target mRNAs by promoting nuclear to cytoplasmic transport of bound transcripts (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data shown in Figure 3B and 3C.

claim: Upon knockdown of YTHDC1, nuclear accumulation of nascent mRNA was observed for APC transcripts.
source: Upon knockdown of YTHDC1, we observed nuclear accumulation of nascent mRNA for both APC and MCL1 transcripts compared to control, whereas the difference in nuclear SOX12 mRNA abundance was modest and not significant in our assay (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Upon knockdown of YTHDC1, nuclear accumulation of nascent mRNA was observed for MCL1 transcripts.
source: Upon knockdown of YTHDC1, we observed nuclear accumulation of nascent mRNA for both APC and MCL1 transcripts compared to control, whereas the difference in nuclear SOX12 mRNA abundance was modest and not significant in our assay (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The difference in nuclear SOX12 mRNA abundance upon YTHDC1 knockdown was modest and not significant.
source: Upon knockdown of YTHDC1, we observed nuclear accumulation of nascent mRNA for both APC and MCL1 transcripts compared to control, whereas the difference in nuclear SOX12 mRNA abundance was modest and not significant in our assay (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Cytoplasmic RNA showed reduced abundance of newly synthesized YTHDC1 targets upon knockdown.
source: Cytoplasmic RNA invariably showed reduced abundance of newly synthesized YTHDC1 targets upon knockdown, suggesting that these transcripts fail to accumulate within the cytoplasm when compared to control levels (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: YTHDC1 is required for proper transport of mature mRNA species from the nucleus to the cytoplasm.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that YTHDC1 is required for proper transport of mature mRNA species from the nucleus to the cytoplasm, as we utilized primer sequences specific for exon-exon junctions of mature transcripts.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data shown in Figure 4A and 4B.

claim: Knockdown of YTHDC1 did not have a significant effect on the distribution of non-target transcripts.
source: Knockdown of YTHDC1 did not have a significant effect on the distribution of non-target transcripts (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: 426 alternative splicing events with a difference in percent spliced in (psi, Ψ) value of 0.2 or greater were identified following knockdown of YTHDC1.
source: Analysis using Mixture of Isoforms (MISO) software (Katz et al., 2010) identified 426 alternative splicing events with a difference in percent spliced in (psi, Ψ) value of 0.2 or greater (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A, Materials and methods).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The alternative splicing events observed following knockdown of YTHDC1 show only weak negative correlations to those observed following knockdown of METTL3.
source: However, the alternative splicing events observed following knockdown of YTHDC1 show only weak negative correlations to those observed following knockdown of METTL3 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B) (Alarcón et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B and comparison to published data.

claim: 85 of 426 alternative splicing events occur in high confidence YTHDC1 targets (11.5%).
source: Of these 426 alternative splicing events, 85 occur in our high confidence YTHDC1 targets (85/737, 11.5%, Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C.

claim: 108 of 426 alternative splicing events occur in YTHDC1 non-targets (2.2%).
source: 108 of the 426 alternative splicing events occur in YTHDC1 non-targets (108/4,848, 2.2%, Figure 4—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Individual transcripts of APC and MCL1 do not show significant changes in alternative exon usage following knockdown of YTHDC1.
source: In addition, individual transcripts of APC and MCL1 do not show significant changes in alternative exon usage following knockdown of YTHDC1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2E), whereas SOX12 mRNA has only one isoform and is therefore not a candidate for regulation by potential alternative splicing events.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2E.

claim: SOX12 mRNA has only one isoform.
source: In addition, individual transcripts of APC and MCL1 do not show significant changes in alternative exon usage following knockdown of YTHDC1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2E), whereas SOX12 mRNA has only one isoform and is therefore not a candidate for regulation by potential alternative splicing events.
evidence: This is stated as a fact in the manuscript.

claim: YTHDC1 does affect alternative splicing patterns.
source: These results show that YTHDC1 does affect alternative splicing patterns, but may play limited roles in alternative splice site selection in HeLa cells (Ke et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data and supported by a citation.

claim: YTHDC1 may play limited roles in alternative splice site selection in HeLa cells.
source: These results show that YTHDC1 does affect alternative splicing patterns, but may play limited roles in alternative splice site selection in HeLa cells (Ke et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data and supported by a citation.

claim: When bound by YTHDC1 rather than by a G-S-S control effector, an increase in Firefly/Renilla luciferase signal was observed.
source: When bound by YTHDC1 rather than by a G-S-S control effector, we observed an increase in Firefly/Renilla luciferase signal (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The effect of YTHDC1 on luciferase expression occurs independent of m6A binding.
source: This effect occurs independent of m6A binding and it is maintained for the W377A mutant construct (Figure 4—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3D.

claim: Binding by YTHDC1 favors mRNA distribution to the cytoplasm.
source: Analysis of mRNA distribution 4 hr after the induction of transcription showed that binding by YTHDC1 favors mRNA distribution to the cytoplasm: we observed decreased mRNA levels of Firefly/Renilla mRNA in the nucleus, and increased ratios in the cytoplasm (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Tethering of the C-terminal effector of YTHDC1 produced increased translation of the Firefly reporter construct.
source: Tethering of the C-terminal effector also produced increased translation of the Firefly reporter construct (Figure 4E), and biased the mRNA distribution of the Firefly transcript towards the cytoplasm (Figure 4F), despite both the full-length and C-terminal constructs being strictly localized to the nucleus (Figure 4—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Tethering of the C-terminal effector of YTHDC1 biased the mRNA distribution of the Firefly transcript towards the cytoplasm.
source: Tethering of the C-terminal effector also produced increased translation of the Firefly reporter construct (Figure 4E), and biased the mRNA distribution of the Firefly transcript towards the cytoplasm (Figure 4F), despite both the full-length and C-terminal constructs being strictly localized to the nucleus (Figure 4—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Both the full-length and C-terminal constructs of YTHDC1 are strictly localized to the nucleus.
source: Tethering of the C-terminal effector also produced increased translation of the Firefly reporter construct (Figure 4E), and biased the mRNA distribution of the Firefly transcript towards the cytoplasm (Figure 4F), despite both the full-length and C-terminal constructs being strictly localized to the nucleus (Figure 4—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3C.

claim: Tethering by the N-terminal construct of YTHDC1 produced no significant change in translation.
source: Tethering by the N-terminal construct produced no significant change in translation, although Firefly mRNA is retained in the nucleus upon binding by this construct (Figure 4—figure supplement 3E and F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3E.

claim: Firefly mRNA is retained in the nucleus upon binding by the N-terminal construct of YTHDC1.
source: Tethering by the N-terminal construct produced no significant change in translation, although Firefly mRNA is retained in the nucleus upon binding by this construct (Figure 4—figure supplement 3E and F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3F.

claim: The N-terminus of YTHDC1 has roles in pre-mRNA splicing.
source: This result is consistent with roles for the N-terminus of YTHDC1 in pre-mRNA splicing and function of the XIST non-coding RNA (Patil et al., 2016; Xiao et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: The N-terminus of YTHDC1 has roles in function of the XIST non-coding RNA.
source: This result is consistent with roles for the N-terminus of YTHDC1 in pre-mRNA splicing and function of the XIST non-coding RNA (Patil et al., 2016; Xiao et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: The effects of binding by the C-terminal region of YTHDC1 represent a new role for YTHDC1 in mRNA export.
source: The effects of binding by the C-terminal region of YTHDC1 represent a new role for YTHDC1 in mRNA export.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on experimental data from the reporter assay.

claim: YTHDC1 is known to interact with members of the SR protein family.
source: YTHDC1 is known to interact with members of the SR protein family, which play diverse roles in pre-mRNA splicing and export (Huang and Steitz, 2001; Huang et al., 2003; Müller-McNicoll et al., 2016; Xiao et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: SR protein family members play diverse roles in pre-mRNA splicing and export.
source: YTHDC1 is known to interact with members of the SR protein family, which play diverse roles in pre-mRNA splicing and export (Huang and Steitz, 2001; Huang et al., 2003; Müller-McNicoll et al., 2016; Xiao et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: YTHDC1 does not directly interact with the export receptor NXF1.
source: Although YTHDC1 interacts with SRSF3, we did not observe any direct interaction between YTHDC1 and the export receptor NXF1, nor did we observe interaction between YTHDC1 and the common mRNA adaptor protein ALYREF (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: YTHDC1 does not interact with the common mRNA adaptor protein ALYREF.
source: Although YTHDC1 interacts with SRSF3, we did not observe any direct interaction between YTHDC1 and the export receptor NXF1, nor did we observe interaction between YTHDC1 and the common mRNA adaptor protein ALYREF (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: SRSF3 is known to interact with both the splicing and the export machinery.
source: Indeed, SRSF3 is known to interact with both the splicing and the export machinery, and is known to do so in a phosphorylation-dependent manner, with hypo-phosphorylated protein interacting with the export receptor (Huang et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: SRSF3 interacts with the export machinery in a phosphorylation-dependent manner.
source: Indeed, SRSF3 is known to interact with both the splicing and the export machinery, and is known to do so in a phosphorylation-dependent manner, with hypo-phosphorylated protein interacting with the export receptor (Huang et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: Hypo-phosphorylated SRSF3 interacts with the export receptor.
source: Indeed, SRSF3 is known to interact with both the splicing and the export machinery, and is known to do so in a phosphorylation-dependent manner, with hypo-phosphorylated protein interacting with the export receptor (Huang et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: YTHDC1 IP samples did not detect phosphorylation at the molecular weight of SRSF3.
source: When probing for serine phosphorylation in YTHDC1 IP samples, we did not detect phosphorylation at the molecular weight of SRSF3, indicating interaction between YTHDC1 and an export-competent form of SRSF3 that lacks serine phosphorylation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: YTHDC1 interacts with an export-competent form of SRSF3 that lacks serine phosphorylation.
source: When probing for serine phosphorylation in YTHDC1 IP samples, we did not detect phosphorylation at the molecular weight of SRSF3, indicating interaction between YTHDC1 and an export-competent form of SRSF3 that lacks serine phosphorylation.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: SRSF3 robustly interacts with YTHDC1 in the presence and absence of RNA.
source: SRSF3 robustly interacts with YTHDC1 in the presence and absence of RNA, whereas NXF1 shows no direct interaction with YTHDC1 but is able to co-precipitate SRSF3 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: NXF1 shows no direct interaction with YTHDC1.
source: SRSF3 robustly interacts with YTHDC1 in the presence and absence of RNA, whereas NXF1 shows no direct interaction with YTHDC1 but is able to co-precipitate SRSF3 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: NXF1 is able to co-precipitate SRSF3.
source: SRSF3 robustly interacts with YTHDC1 in the presence and absence of RNA, whereas NXF1 shows no direct interaction with YTHDC1 but is able to co-precipitate SRSF3 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The C-terminus of YTHDC1 interacts with endogenous SRSF3 in an RNA-independent manner.
source: Indeed, we observed an RNA-independent interaction between endogenous SRSF3 and the C-terminus of YTHDC1, but did not observe an interaction between endogenous SRSF3 and the N-terminus of YTHDC1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The N-terminus of YTHDC1 does not interact with endogenous SRSF3.
source: Indeed, we observed an RNA-independent interaction between endogenous SRSF3 and the C-terminus of YTHDC1, but did not observe an interaction between endogenous SRSF3 and the N-terminus of YTHDC1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Both SRSF3 and NXF1 can enrich m6A compared to input.
source: We found that both SRSF3 and NXF1 are able to enrich m6A compared to input, with SRSF3 producing the greatest enrichment (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: SRSF3 produces the greatest enrichment of m6A compared to NXF1.
source: We found that both SRSF3 and NXF1 are able to enrich m6A compared to input, with SRSF3 producing the greatest enrichment (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The RNA recognition motif of SRSF3 showed no selectivity for m6A in vitro.
source: Although the protein could enrich for m6A when immunoprecipitated from cells, the RNA recognition motif of SRSF3 showed no selectivity for m6A in vitro (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Knockdown of SRSF3 leads to a large increase in nuclear m6A levels.
source: We find that knockdown of SRSF3 leads to a large increase in nuclear m6A levels, whereas other members of the SR protein family that interact with YTHDC1 show only modest changes in m6A levels in the nucleus or cytoplasm upon knockdown (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Other members of the SR protein family that interact with YTHDC1 show only modest changes in m6A levels in the nucleus or cytoplasm upon knockdown.
source: We find that knockdown of SRSF3 leads to a large increase in nuclear m6A levels, whereas other members of the SR protein family that interact with YTHDC1 show only modest changes in m6A levels in the nucleus or cytoplasm upon knockdown (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–C.

claim: Depletion of HNRNPA2B1 and HNRNPC does not significantly affect subcellular m6A levels in a manner consistent with a role in mRNA export.
source: Depletion of the other nuclear reader proteins HNRNPA2B1 and HNRNPC does not significantly affect subcellular m6A levels in a manner consistent with a role in mRNA export (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–C.

claim: Knockdown of SRSF3 results in increased nuclear staining of polyA RNAs and decreased cytoplasmic signal.
source: Like knockdown of YTHDC1, knockdown of SRSF3 results in increased nuclear staining of polyA RNAs and decreased cytoplasmic signal (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2D.

claim: SRSF3 facilitates the export of m6A-methylated mRNAs via interaction with both YTHDC1 and NXF1.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that SRSF3 facilitates the export of m6A-methylated mRNAs via interaction with both the m6A-selective protein and YTHDC1 and the canonical mRNA export receptor NXF1, and that SRSF3 may contribute to additional fates for modified nuclear transcripts.
evidence: This is an inference based on multiple lines of experimental data including protein interactions, CLIP-seq, and subcellular localization studies.

claim: SRSF3 may contribute to additional fates for modified nuclear transcripts.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that SRSF3 facilitates the export of m6A-methylated mRNAs via interaction with both the m6A-selective protein and YTHDC1 and the canonical mRNA export receptor NXF1, and that SRSF3 may contribute to additional fates for modified nuclear transcripts.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation of enriched nuclear m6A upon SRSF3 knockdown.

claim: YTHDC1 is a limiting protein in the mRNA export system.
source: According to the results of both RNA-sequencing (our data) and proteomic studies (Nagaraj et al., 2011), YTHDC1 is a limiting protein in this system (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and a citation to prior published work.

claim: Knockdown of YTHDC1, SRSF3, or METTL3/14 results in nuclear accumulation of YTHDC1 targets.
source: Knockdown of YTHDC1, SRSF3, or the methyltransferase components METTL3/14 results in nuclear accumulation of YTHDC1 targets without affecting non-target HPRT1 mRNA (Figure 5—figure supplement 4A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4B.

claim: Knockdown of YTHDC1, SRSF3, or METTL3/14 does not affect non-target HPRT1 mRNA in the nucleus.
source: Knockdown of YTHDC1, SRSF3, or the methyltransferase components METTL3/14 results in nuclear accumulation of YTHDC1 targets without affecting non-target HPRT1 mRNA (Figure 5—figure supplement 4A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4B.

claim: Knockdown of YTHDC1 or SRSF3 reduces cytoplasmic levels of YTHDC1 targets.
source: In the cytoplasm, knockdown of either YTHDC1 or SRSF3 reduces levels of YTHDC1 targets, whereas depletion of the methyltransferase results in significant accumulations – probably as a result of reduced cytoplasmic clearance of transcripts bearing reduced m6A through YTHDF2 (Figure 5—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4C.

claim: Depletion of the methyltransferase METTL3/14 results in significant accumulations of YTHDC1 targets in the cytoplasm.
source: In the cytoplasm, knockdown of either YTHDC1 or SRSF3 reduces levels of YTHDC1 targets, whereas depletion of the methyltransferase results in significant accumulations – probably as a result of reduced cytoplasmic clearance of transcripts bearing reduced m6A through YTHDF2 (Figure 5—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4C.

claim: Cytoplasmic accumulation of YTHDC1 targets upon METTL3/14 knockdown is probably a result of reduced cytoplasmic clearance of transcripts bearing reduced m6A through YTHDF2.
source: In the cytoplasm, knockdown of either YTHDC1 or SRSF3 reduces levels of YTHDC1 targets, whereas depletion of the methyltransferase results in significant accumulations – probably as a result of reduced cytoplasmic clearance of transcripts bearing reduced m6A through YTHDF2 (Figure 5—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data and prior knowledge of YTHDF2 function.

claim: The YTH domain of YTHDC1 binds mRNA with preference for m6A.
source: The YTH domain of YTHDC1 has been extensively biochemically characterized as a nuclear 'reader' protein, and binds mRNA with preference for m6A (Xu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: YTHDC1 is required for RNA binding by SRSF3.
source: Previous work has suggested that YTHDC1 is required for RNA binding by SRSF3, consistent with a role for YTHDC1 in facilitating mRNA export selectivity (Xiao et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: Knockdown of YTHDC1 reduced enrichment of m6A by SRSF3.
source: We observed enrichment of m6A in mRNA bound by SRSF3 under both conditions. However, knockdown of YTHDC1 reduced enrichment of m6A by SRSF3, suggesting that YTHDC1 partially facilitates substrate selection by SRSF3 (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: YTHDC1 partially facilitates substrate selection by SRSF3.
source: We observed enrichment of m6A in mRNA bound by SRSF3 under both conditions. However, knockdown of YTHDC1 reduced enrichment of m6A by SRSF3, suggesting that YTHDC1 partially facilitates substrate selection by SRSF3 (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Knockdown of YTHDC1 reduced target transcript enrichment by SRSF3.
source: Sequencing of SRSF3-bound RNAs under control and knockdown conditions further supports this role of YTHDC1, as knockdown of YTHDC1 reduced target transcript enrichment of SRSF3 (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Knockdown of YTHDC1 abolished m6A enrichment by NXF1.
source: Similarly, knockdown of YTHDC1 abolished m6A enrichment by NXF1 as determined by LC-MS/MS (Figure 6C) and reduced transcript enrichment as determined by NXF1 RIP-seq (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Knockdown of YTHDC1 reduced transcript enrichment by NXF1.
source: Similarly, knockdown of YTHDC1 abolished m6A enrichment by NXF1 as determined by LC-MS/MS (Figure 6C) and reduced transcript enrichment as determined by NXF1 RIP-seq (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: YTHDC1 is required for proper incorporation of methylated mRNA targets into mRNPs consisting of SRSF3 and NXF1.
source: These data show that YTHDC1 is required for proper incorporation of methylated mRNA targets into mRNPs consisting of SRSF3 and NXF1, which together function to facilitate nuclear export of their RNA cargo.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: SRSF3 and NXF1 together function to facilitate nuclear export of their RNA cargo.
source: These data show that YTHDC1 is required for proper incorporation of methylated mRNA targets into mRNPs consisting of SRSF3 and NXF1, which together function to facilitate nuclear export of their RNA cargo.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge and the experimental data presented.

claim: SRSF3 and other members of the SR protein family interact directly with the export receptor NXF1.
source: Our data suggest that SRSF3 serves as a key adaptor in mediating the export of mRNA bound by YTHDC1, as SRSF3 and other members of the SR protein family interact directly with the export receptor NXF1 (Huang et al., 2003; Müller-McNicoll et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Only transcripts bound by both YTHDC1 and SRSF3 show significant nuclear accumulation upon YTHDC1 knockdown.
source: We analyzed subcellular RNA-seq data following knockdown of YTHDC1 according to these transcript groupings, and found that only transcripts bound by both YTHDC1 and SRSF3 show significant nuclear accumulation upon YTHDC1 knockdown, whereas transcripts bound by YTHDC1 but not SRSF3 show no significant nuclear accumulation when comparing mean abundance (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Transcripts bound by YTHDC1 but not SRSF3 show no significant nuclear accumulation upon YTHDC1 knockdown.
source: We analyzed subcellular RNA-seq data following knockdown of YTHDC1 according to these transcript groupings, and found that only transcripts bound by both YTHDC1 and SRSF3 show significant nuclear accumulation upon YTHDC1 knockdown, whereas transcripts bound by YTHDC1 but not SRSF3 show no significant nuclear accumulation when comparing mean abundance (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Cytoplasmic depletion following knockdown of YTHDC1 depends on SRSF3 binding.
source: We observe a similar dependence on SRSF3 binding in cytoplasmic depletion following knockdown of YTHDC1, indicating a functional role for binding by both YTHDC1 and SRSF3 as opposed to YTHDC1 binding alone (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: SRSF3 serves as an export adapter for methylated nuclear mRNAs bound by both YTHDC1 and SRSF3.
source: Our data suggest that SRSF3 serves as an export adapter for methylated nuclear mRNAs bound by both YTHDC1 and SRSF3.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: SRSF3 forms the functional protein–RNA complex for selective association with NXF1 for export to the cytoplasm.
source: This study provides a basis for distinct nuclear fates for mRNAs that are bound by YTHDC1 in which a downstream adaptor protein — here, SRSF3 – forms the functional protein–RNA complex for selective association with NXF1 for export to the cytoplasm (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: The knockdown of YTHDC1 results in defective nuclear export of target mRNAs in an m6A-dependent, splicing-independent manner.
source: The knockdown of YTHDC1 results in defective nuclear export of target mRNAs, and does so in an m6A-dependent, splicing-independent manner.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the reporter assay and analysis of splicing-independent effects.

claim: Binding of YTHDC1 to target transcripts is sufficient to facilitate nuclear export.
source: Binding of YTHDC1 to target transcripts is sufficient to facilitate nuclear export, which indirectly leads to increased translation by increasing the cytoplasmic abundance of its targets.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the reporter assay (Figure 4).

claim: Binding of YTHDC1 indirectly leads to increased translation by increasing the cytoplasmic abundance of its targets.
source: Binding of YTHDC1 to target transcripts is sufficient to facilitate nuclear export, which indirectly leads to increased translation by increasing the cytoplasmic abundance of its targets.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data from the reporter assay (Figure 4).

claim: The interaction between YTHDC1 and SRSF3 couples m6A selectivity to nuclear export.
source: The interaction between YTHDC1 and SRSF3 couples m6A selectivity to nuclear export, in which m6A binding by YTHDC1 propagates transport via NXF1 involving the adaptor SRSF3, which itself does not impart biochemical selectivity for m6A in vitro.
evidence: This is an inference based on multiple lines of experimental data including protein interactions, CLIP-seq, and in vitro binding assays.

claim: SRSF3 does not impart biochemical selectivity for m6A in vitro.
source: The interaction between YTHDC1 and SRSF3 couples m6A selectivity to nuclear export, in which m6A binding by YTHDC1 propagates transport via NXF1 involving the adaptor SRSF3, which itself does not impart biochemical selectivity for m6A in vitro.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: YTHDC1 knockdown results in decreased association of target mRNAs with both SRSF3 and NXF1.
source: YTHDC1 knockdown results in decreased association of target mRNAs with both SRSF3 and NXF1, indicating that YTHDC1 is partially responsible for substrate selection by components of the mRNA export pathway.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: YTHDC1 is partially responsible for substrate selection by components of the mRNA export pathway.
source: YTHDC1 knockdown results in decreased association of target mRNAs with both SRSF3 and NXF1, indicating that YTHDC1 is partially responsible for substrate selection by components of the mRNA export pathway.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: m6A methylation in mRNA occurs co-transcriptionally.
source: Although m6A methylation in mRNA occurs co-transcriptionally, processes that select for methylated mRNAs within the nucleus are still under investigation.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Processes that select for methylated mRNAs within the nucleus are still under investigation.
source: Although m6A methylation in mRNA occurs co-transcriptionally, processes that select for methylated mRNAs within the nucleus are still under investigation.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field at the time of writing.

claim: Mechanisms that maintain efficient processing and export of nascent transcripts are critical to enable proper gene expression.
source: Mechanisms that maintain efficient processing and export of nascent transcripts are critical to enable proper gene expression, given that the vast majority of RNA transcribed in the nucleus is degraded prior to nuclear export (Moore, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: The vast majority of RNA transcribed in the nucleus is degraded prior to nuclear export.
source: Mechanisms that maintain efficient processing and export of nascent transcripts are critical to enable proper gene expression, given that the vast majority of RNA transcribed in the nucleus is degraded prior to nuclear export (Moore, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: YTHDC1 can affect the transport of mRNAs from the nucleus in addition to roles in pre-mRNA splicing.
source: Although YTHDC1 has been shown to affect alternative splicing of select mRNAs (Rafalska et al., 2004; Xiao et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2010), our data suggest that YTHDC1 can affect the transport of mRNAs from the nucleus in addition to roles in pre-mRNA splicing.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data presented in the manuscript and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The results are consistent with the tight biochemical coupling of mRNA splicing and export.
source: These results are consistent with the tight biochemical coupling of mRNA splicing and export, and are reminiscent of the dual roles observed for similar adaptor proteins, particularly those of the SR-family which have been well documented (Huang and Steitz, 2001; Huang et al., 2003; Müller-McNicoll et al., 2016; Strässer and Hurt, 2001; Valencia et al., 2008; Zhou et al., 2000).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on experimental data and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: This work reveals a mechanism by which methylated mRNAs are selectively incorporated into known pathways for mRNA export.
source: This work reveals a mechanism by which methylated mRNAs are selectively incorporated into known pathways for mRNA export.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings of the study.

claim: YTHDC1 binds to mRNA within the nucleus in an m6A-selective manner.
source: We propose a model in which YTHDC1 binds to mRNA within the nucleus in an m6A-selective manner, and then delivers target mRNA to SRSF3.
evidence: This is a model based on experimental data and prior knowledge of YTHDC1's m6A-binding properties.

claim: YTHDC1 delivers target mRNA to SRSF3.
source: We propose a model in which YTHDC1 binds to mRNA within the nucleus in an m6A-selective manner, and then delivers target mRNA to SRSF3.
evidence: This is a model based on experimental data showing protein interactions and effects on RNA binding.

claim: Upon association with SRSF3, binding of mRNA by YTHDC1 mediates nuclear export.
source: Upon association with SRSF3, binding of mRNA by YTHDC1 mediates nuclear export.
evidence: This is a model based on experimental data showing functional dependence on SRSF3 for export.

claim: SRSF3 associates with spliceosomal components prior to release by dephosphorylation.
source: SRSF3 associates with spliceosomal components prior to release by dephosphorylation, at which point the mRNP interacts with the export receptor (Huang et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: YTHDC1 incorporates bound mRNAs into a dephosphorylated SRSF3-containing complex, facilitating their export.
source: Our model suggests that YTHDC1 incorporates bound mRNAs into a dephosphorylated SRSF3-containing complex, facilitating their export.
evidence: This is a model based on experimental data showing interaction with hypo-phosphorylated SRSF3.

claim: YTHDC1 binds target RNA and delivers it to SRSF3 in a pathway separate from co-transcriptional binding in association with the spliceosome.
source: In each case, we propose that YTHDC1 binds target RNA and delivers it to SRSF3 in a pathway separate from co-transcriptional binding in association with the spliceosome.
evidence: This is a model based on experimental data and speculation about the mechanism.

claim: It is unlikely that YTHDC1 acts entirely upstream of SR-proteins given the relative stoichiometry of YTHDC1 and SRSF3.
source: Given the relative stoichiometry of YTHDC1 and SRSF3, it is unlikely that YTHDC1 acts entirely upstream of SR-proteins, yet our data suggest that YTHDC1 assists in delivering a subset of SRSF3 RNA cargo, namely methylated mRNAs, for export via NXF1.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data showing protein abundance and functional data.

claim: YTHDC1 assists in delivering a subset of SRSF3 RNA cargo, namely methylated mRNAs, for export via NXF1.
source: Given the relative stoichiometry of YTHDC1 and SRSF3, it is unlikely that YTHDC1 acts entirely upstream of SR-proteins, yet our data suggest that YTHDC1 assists in delivering a subset of SRSF3 RNA cargo, namely methylated mRNAs, for export via NXF1.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data showing selective effects on YTHDC1 targets.

claim: Alternative mechanisms could operate for the selective processing of m6A-methylated transcripts in which interactions between SR-proteins and components of the methyltransferase during transcription may also contribute to diverse outcomes for methylated transcripts within the nucleus.
source: Critically, alternative mechanisms could operate for the selective processing of m6A-methylated transcripts in which interactions between SR-proteins and components of the methyltransferase during transcription may also contribute to diverse outcomes for methylated transcripts within the nucleus (Schwartz et al., 2014), as indicated by enriched nuclear m6A methylation upon SRSF3 knockdown.
evidence: This is speculation based on experimental observations and supported by a citation.

claim: YTHDC1 and SRSF3 do not function exclusively in mediating mRNA export.
source: YTHDC1 and SRSF3 do not function exclusively in mediating mRNA export, but the incorporation of SRSF3 to form an export-competent mRNP is critical to facilitate mRNA trafficking to the cytoplasm after binding by YTHDC1.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data and prior knowledge of these proteins' multiple functions.

claim: The incorporation of SRSF3 to form an export-competent mRNP is critical to facilitate mRNA trafficking to the cytoplasm after binding by YTHDC1.
source: YTHDC1 and SRSF3 do not function exclusively in mediating mRNA export, but the incorporation of SRSF3 to form an export-competent mRNP is critical to facilitate mRNA trafficking to the cytoplasm after binding by YTHDC1.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data showing functional dependence on SRSF3.

claim: Depletion of YTHDC1 favors exon skipping.
source: Depletion of YTHDC1 favors exon skipping, potentially resulting from prolonged nuclear lifetime enabling more extensive pre-mRNA processing.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data and speculation about the mechanism.

claim: Exon skipping upon YTHDC1 depletion potentially results from prolonged nuclear lifetime enabling more extensive pre-mRNA processing.
source: Depletion of YTHDC1 favors exon skipping, potentially resulting from prolonged nuclear lifetime enabling more extensive pre-mRNA processing.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism underlying the observed effect.

claim: Perturbation of YTHDC1 levels may affect the localization of SR-proteins.
source: Additionally, perturbation of YTHDC1 levels may affect the localization of SR-proteins (Xiao et al., 2016) and prevent access to certain pre-mRNAs.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: Perturbation of YTHDC1 levels may prevent access to certain pre-mRNAs.
source: Additionally, perturbation of YTHDC1 levels may affect the localization of SR-proteins (Xiao et al., 2016) and prevent access to certain pre-mRNAs.
evidence: This is speculation about potential mechanisms.

claim: m6A methylation serves as a mark for selective nuclear processing.
source: In this study, we show that m6A methylation serves as a mark for selective nuclear processing, and identify a unique role for YTHDC1 in mediating selectivity in this fundamental component of eukaryotic gene expression.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental findings of the study.

claim: m6A in mRNA serves to facilitate critical steps in mRNA metabolism, enhancing translation initiation and mRNA decay in the cytoplasm.
source: Current data suggest that m6A in mRNA serves to facilitate critical steps in mRNA metabolism, enhancing translation initiation and mRNA decay in the cytoplasm (Du et al., 2016; Lin et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2014a, 2014b, , 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Selective RNA turnover is common to both nuclear and cytoplasmic mRNA.
source: Our work shows that selective RNA turnover is common to both nuclear and cytoplasmic mRNA, whereby methylation facilitates mRNA export prior to translation initiation and eventual mRNA decay.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Methylation facilitates mRNA export prior to translation initiation and eventual mRNA decay.
source: Our work shows that selective RNA turnover is common to both nuclear and cytoplasmic mRNA, whereby methylation facilitates mRNA export prior to translation initiation and eventual mRNA decay.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Findings contribute to pathways for m6A-dependent mRNA metabolism by establishing a mechanistic basis for preferential nuclear processing and export of methylated mRNAs by YTHDC1.
source: Findings presented here contribute to pathways for m6A-dependent mRNA metabolism by establishing a mechanistic basis for preferential nuclear processing and export of methylated mRNAs by YTHDC1.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main contribution of the study.
